title: Git Rebase: Rewriting History Safely
summary: A study-notes series on git rebase: how it differs from merge, how commits are replayed, interactive rebase, autosquash, conflict handling, --onto, force-with-lease on shared branches, and recovery with reflog and rerere.

chapters.title: Rebase vs Merge
points: Merge joins two histories with a new merge commit that has two parents; history stays a true DAG
Rebase replays your commits on top of another base, producing a linear history with no merge commit
Rebase creates NEW commits with new SHAs; the old commits still exist until garbage collected
Merge preserves context (when the branch diverged); rebase preserves readability (a straight line)
Fast-forward merge: if the target has no new commits, merge just moves the pointer, no merge commit
git switch feature && git rebase main puts feature's commits after main's tip
After rebasing, a fast-forward merge into main gives a clean linear history
git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible
Merge is non-destructive; rebase rewrites history, so it is a trade-off, not a replacement
git pull --rebase replaces the fetch+merge of a default pull with fetch+rebase
Set pull.rebase=true to make rebase the default for git pull
Rule of thumb: rebase to tidy your own local work, merge to integrate shared work

chapters.title: How Commits Are Replayed
points: A commit is a snapshot plus parent pointer, author, message; changing the parent changes the SHA
Step 1: find the merge-base of the current branch and the upstream
Step 2: collect the commits in upstream..HEAD (reachable from HEAD, not upstream)
Step 3: detach HEAD and checkout the upstream tip
Step 4: cherry-pick each commit in order, applying its diff as a three-way merge
Step 5: move the branch name to the final new commit and drop the old pointer
Each replayed commit keeps author and message but gets a new committer date and SHA
Descendant commits all get new SHAs because each parent hash is part of the child hash
Commits already present upstream (same patch-id) are skipped automatically
git range-diff old..new compares the original series to the rebased series
ORIG_HEAD records the branch tip before the rebase started
During a rebase HEAD is detached; state lives in .git/rebase-merge/

chapters.title: Interactive Rebase Basics
points: git rebase -i HEAD~4 opens an editor listing the last 4 commits, oldest first
Order is oldest at top, the opposite of git log, because commits replay top to bottom
pick: keep the commit unchanged
reword: keep the changes, stop to edit the commit message
edit: stop after applying the commit so you can amend or split it, then --continue
squash: meld into the previous commit and combine both messages
fixup: meld into the previous commit and discard this message
drop: delete the commit (or just remove its line)
Reordering lines reorders commits; conflicts may appear if they touch the same code
git rebase -i --root lets you rewrite the very first commit too
Deleting every line (empty todo) aborts the rebase
exec lines run a shell command, e.g. exec npm test, after a commit

chapters.title: Squash, Fixup, Reword, Edit in Practice
points: Squash a WIP series: keep the first pick, mark the rest squash or fixup
squash opens an editor to merge messages; fixup silently keeps the earlier message
Reword fixes a typo in an old message without touching the code
Edit stops at the commit; run git commit --amend to change it, then git rebase --continue
Split a commit: mark edit, git reset HEAD^, stage in pieces with git add -p, commit each, continue
Drop a commit that added debug code or a bad experiment
Example todo: pick a1b2c3 Add login / fixup d4e5f6 typo / squash 7a8b9c tests / reword 0f1e2d msg
Use git commit --amend only for the latest commit; interactive rebase for older ones
Reorder to group related fixes next to their targets before squashing
Keep each final commit atomic: one logical change that builds and passes tests
Rewrite only unpushed or personal-branch commits to avoid disrupting teammates
Run git log --oneline before and after to verify the result

chapters.title: Autosquash and fixup! Commits
points: git commit --fixup=<sha> creates a commit titled fixup! <original subject>
git commit --squash=<sha> creates squash! <subject>, and --fixup=reword:<sha> rewords on autosquash
git rebase -i --autosquash moves each fixup!/squash! line under its target and sets the action
Workflow: commit fixes as you review, then autosquash once before merging
git config rebase.autoSquash true makes --autosquash the default for -i
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main targets everything since main
Matching is by subject prefix or by SHA, so renaming the target commit breaks the match
Combine with GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=true to accept the todo without opening an editor
Example: git commit --fixup=a1b2c3 then git rebase -i --autosquash a1b2c3^
Fixup targets must be in the rebase range or they stay as plain commits
amend!-style commits (--fixup=amend:<sha>) replace both content and message
Autosquash only reorders the todo; you still review it before saving

chapters.title: Resolving Conflicts: --continue, --abort, --skip
points: Conflicts happen because each replayed commit is a three-way merge that may not apply cleanly
Rebase pauses and reports CONFLICT; files show <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> markers
Resolve by editing the files, then git add <file> to mark them resolved
git rebase --continue resumes replay with the next commit
git rebase --abort restores the branch to exactly its pre-rebase state
git rebase --skip discards the current commit entirely, use when upstream already contains it
Do NOT run git commit mid-conflict; just add and --continue (unless in edit mode)
Meaning is flipped: 'ours' is the upstream branch being built on, 'theirs' is your commit being replayed
git checkout --ours/--theirs <file> picks one side wholesale (with the flip in mind)
git status shows 'rebase in progress' and which step, e.g. 3/7
The same conflict may repeat across several commits; later ones get easier or rerere handles them
git mergetool opens a visual three-way resolver
Rebase with many commits means many conflict stops; squash first to resolve once

chapters.title: Moving Branches with --onto
points: Syntax: git rebase --onto <newbase> <oldbase> <branch>
Replays commits in oldbase..branch on top of newbase
Example: topic was branched off feature, move it onto main: git rebase --onto main feature topic
Remove commits from the middle: git rebase --onto A B drops the commits between A and B
Transplant after a squash-merged parent: git rebase --onto main <old-parent-tip> topic
Without --onto, rebase uses the upstream as both the cut point and the new base
The three arguments answer: where to land, where to cut, what to move
Use it when a stacked branch's parent was squash-merged and diverged from your copy
Omitting <branch> rebases the currently checked-out branch
After --onto, the old base branch is untouched; only the named branch moves
Diagram: A-B-C(main) with D-E(feature) and F-G(topic) becomes F'-G' on C
Verify with git log --graph --oneline --all before and after

chapters.title: Rebasing Shared Branches and force-with-lease
points: Golden rule: never rebase commits that others have already pulled
Rebased commits have new SHAs, so teammates' copies diverge from yours
After rebasing a pushed branch, a normal push is rejected as non-fast-forward
git push --force overwrites the remote blindly and can destroy others' commits
git push --force-with-lease only overwrites if the remote still matches what you last fetched
force-with-lease fails if a teammate pushed meanwhile, protecting their work
Pin it: --force-with-lease=branch:<expected-sha> for stricter safety
Fetching in the background (IDE auto-fetch) can defeat the lease, so fetch deliberately
--force-if-includes adds a check that your local branch integrated the remote tip
Personal feature branches behind a PR are fine to rebase; announce it to reviewers
Protect main with branch protection to block force pushes entirely
Teammate recovery after your force push: git fetch then git rebase --onto origin/branch <old-sha>

chapters.title: Recovery with Reflog and rerere
points: git reflog lists where HEAD and branches pointed over time, even after rewriting
Each entry looks like HEAD@{3}: rebase (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature
Undo a bad rebase: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD or git reset --hard HEAD@{n}
Old commits survive until gc, roughly 90 days for reachable and 30 for unreachable entries
git branch rescue <sha> pins a lost commit before it can be collected
git reflog show feature shows one branch's history
Reflog is local only; it is never pushed or shared
Dropped commits via interactive rebase are recoverable with their SHA from the reflog
rerere = reuse recorded resolution: Git remembers how you resolved a conflict
Enable with git config rerere.enabled true
Next identical conflict is auto-resolved from .git/rr-cache; you still add and continue
Great for long-lived branches rebased repeatedly or for rebase-then-merge experiments
git rerere forget <path> clears a wrong recorded resolution

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
points: Rebasing a public branch like main or a shared develop branch
Force pushing with plain --force instead of --force-with-lease
Running git commit during a conflict instead of --continue
Confusing ours and theirs and keeping the wrong side
Giant rebases with 50 commits; squash or rebase in smaller steps
Forgetting that rebase rewrites SHAs, so references in issues and notes go stale
Losing work by aborting after resolving; use reflog if it happens
Not running tests after rebase; a clean replay can still break behavior
Back up first: git branch backup-feature before a risky rebase
Prefer git pull --rebase locally to avoid noisy merge commits
Use --autostash to stash and reapply uncommitted changes around a rebase
Rebase before opening a PR, merge when integrating shared work

chapters.title: Git Rebase Cheatsheet
points: git rebase main: replay current branch onto main
git rebase -i HEAD~N: edit the last N commits
git rebase -i --autosquash <base>: fold fixup!/squash! commits
git rebase --onto <new> <old> <branch>: transplant a range
git rebase --continue | --abort | --skip: control a paused rebase
git commit --fixup=<sha>: create an autosquash target commit
git push --force-with-lease: safe force push after rewriting
git reflog and git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD: undo a rebase
git config rerere.enabled true: remember conflict resolutions
git config pull.rebase true and rebase.autoSquash true: sensible defaults
todo actions: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, exec
Golden rule: rewrite only commits nobody else has
